title: Data Serialization
description: Compare JSON, XML, and Protocol Buffers — understanding schema evolution, backward compatibility, and performance tradeoffs.

segments.text: Data doesn't travel as objects or structs across the wire. It has to be serialized — flattened into bytes. The format you choose affects performance, readability, and how easily your system evolves over time.

JSON is the king of web APIs. It's human-readable, lightweight, and natively supported by JavaScript. Curly braces, key-value pairs, arrays. Every developer knows it. But it's text-based, which means it's not the most compact.

XML was JSON's predecessor. Verbose, tag-based, with opening and closing tags for everything. It supports namespaces, schemas, and transformations. Enterprise systems still use it heavily, but for new APIs it's largely been replaced by JSON.

Let's compare. The same data in JSON might be two hundred bytes. In XML, four hundred bytes — double the size because of all those closing tags. Field names repeat in every single record. That overhead adds up at scale.

Protocol Buffers — protobuf — take a different approach. You define your schema in a dot-proto file, and a compiler generates code in your language. Data is encoded as compact binary, not text. Field names become tiny integer tags.
That same two-hundred-byte JSON payload? In protobuf it might be fifty bytes. Four times smaller. And parsing is orders of magnitude faster because there's no text to tokenize.
segments.thought_prompt: If protobuf is so much faster and smaller, why isn't everyone using it instead of JSON?

segments.text: The tradeoff is readability. You can't open a protobuf message in a text editor and understand it. Debugging is harder. You need the schema to decode anything. JSON wins for public APIs where developer experience matters most.

Systems change. You'll add fields, remove fields, rename things. Schema evolution is how your format handles these changes. Can old code read new data? Can new code read old data? This is backward and forward compatibility.

JSON handles evolution loosely — unknown fields are simply ignored. Protobuf handles it rigorously — new fields get new tag numbers, old fields are never reused. Both approaches work, but protobuf catches more mistakes at compile time.
There are other players too. Avro uses schemas but doesn't require code generation. MessagePack is binary JSON. Thrift is Facebook's alternative to protobuf. The landscape is rich.
segments.thought_prompt: When would you choose protobuf over JSON for internal service-to-service communication?

segments.text: JSON for public APIs and human readability. Protobuf for internal services needing speed and compactness. XML for legacy enterprise systems. Pick the right format for your context, and always plan for schema evolution from day one.
